bio.en: Fareed Mosavat is the Chief Development Officer at Reforge and a veteran product leader who, before Reforge, led growth at Slack and Instacart, served as VP of Product at Runkeeper and GM at Zynga, and spent six years building 3D animation tools at Pixar.
bio.zh: Fareed Mosavat 是 Reforge 的首席发展官（Chief Development Officer），也是一位资深产品负责人；在加入 Reforge 之前，他曾在 Slack 和 Instacart 主导增长，担任 Runkeeper 的产品副总裁、Zynga 的总经理，并在皮克斯工作了六年，开发 3D 动画工具。

summary.en: Fareed argues that the only way to get better at product management is to do the real work—shipping real products for real customers with real data—because training, mentorship, and reading are merely layers on top of raw repetition. He walks through the difficult transition from individual contributor to manager, emphasizing that crossing 'the canyon' requires deliberately expanding your scope and owning outcomes rather than tasks. A core theme is creating opportunities to take on more responsibility: great PMs accelerate by seeking out the highest-leverage work and proving they can handle bigger bets. He also shares practical advice on how to build the reps that compound into senior product judgment, making this a field guide for any PM who wants to level up from solid executor to influential leader.
summary.zh: Fareed 认为，提升产品管理能力唯一的途径就是去做真正的工作——为真实的客户、用真实的数据去交付真实的产品——因为培训、导师指导和阅读都只是在大量重复练习之上的一层包装。他拆解了从一线执行者（IC）到管理者那段艰难的跨越，强调跨过这道“峡谷”需要刻意扩大自己的影响范围，并对结果而非任务负责。一个核心主题是创造机会去承担更多责任：优秀的 PM 会主动去寻找杠杆最高的事情，并证明自己能扛得起更大的赌注，从而加速成长。他还分享了如何通过一次次实战积累出高阶产品判断力的实用建议，对每一位想从靠谱执行者进阶为有影响力的领导者 PM 来说，这都是一份实战指南。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: You can't do homework. You can't do exercises. You can't do fake stuff. You have to work on real products at real companies with real customers, with real data to get better at product management. So any kind of training, mentorship, reading, et cetera that you do is just a layer on top of that. The real acceleration happens from doing it and getting more reps. There are ways that I think great PMs use to go faster on this loop, but you still have to do the work. At the core is you have to actually execute and deliver great products, and you have to do it over, and over, and over again.
turns.zh: 你不能做作业。你不能做练习。你不能做假事。你必须在真实的​​公司、真实的客户、真实的数据上开发真实的产品，才能更好地进行产品管理。因此，你所做的任何类型的培训、指导、阅读等都只是在此之上的一层。真正的加速来自于做这件事并获得更多次数。我认为优秀的产品经理可以使用一些方法来加快这个循环，但你仍然需要完成工作。核心是你必须实际执行和交付出色的产品，并且你必须一遍又一遍地这样做。

He's a GM at Zynga, he's VP of Product at Runkeeper, and something that I only learned during our chat is that he spent six years at Pixar doing character simulation, rigging, and building 3D animation tools. turns.zh: 因此，为了向不太熟悉您的听众介绍一些背景信息，您能否用 45 秒的时间向我们介绍一下您的职业生涯以及您所做过的所有精彩事情？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Great. Hi. I'm Fareed Mosavat. I live in Berkeley, California with my wonderful wife and two children, but I've been a product leader across a variety of different companies over the course of my career. Today, I am the chief development officer at Reforge where I help run all of our content teams, parts of our operations, and our partnerships with wonderful experts like yourself.
turns.zh: 伟大的。你好。我是法里德·莫萨瓦特。我和我出色的妻子和两个孩子住在加利福尼亚州伯克利，但在我的职业生涯中，我一直是多家不同公司的产品负责人。如今，我是 Reforge 的首席开发官，负责管理我们所有的内容团队、部分运营以及与像您这样的优秀专家的合作关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. What about all the other things you've done?
turns.zh: 惊人的。你做过的所有其他事情又如何呢？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So, previous to this, I spent almost four years as the director of product for a team called Lifecycle at Slack that is effectively a growth team. We're responsible for the self-service business at Slack all the way from first sign up, first team creation through to the first invites, activation, expansion, modernization, and even connecting the dots with our SMB sales team to help nurture some of those small self-service teams into larger commitments through our sales team.
turns.zh: 因此，在此之前，我在 Slack 的一个名为 Lifecycle 的团队中担任了近四年的产品总监，该团队实际上是一个成长团队。我们负责 Slack 的自助服务业务，从首次注册、第一个团队创建到首次邀请、激活、扩展、现代化，甚至与我们的中小企业销售团队联系起来，通过我们的销售团队帮助培养一些小型自助服务团队做出更大的承诺。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: I came to that through a variety of different growth and product leadership roles at a bunch of different startups on larger companies. I built one of the first growth teams at Instacart for about a year and a half in the middle of their acceleration. I was VP of Product at a company called Runkeeper before that in Boston, health and fitness tracking company. I was a general manager at Zynga. I got there through a startup that I was an engineer at, basically started as an engineer, ended as a head of product over the course of a couple of years, and then got acquired into Zynga, and actually started my career with almost seven years at Pixar Animation Studios working on visual effects, software tools, and other creative tech to try and solve problems for a bunch of wonderful films you've probably seen or your kids have seen.
turns.zh: 我是通过在大公司的许多不同初创公司担任各种不同的增长和产品领导角色而实现这一目标的。我在 Instacart 建立了第一批增长团队，花了大约一年半的时间在他们的加速过程中。在此之前，我曾在波士顿一家名为 Runkeeper 的健康和健身追踪公司担任产品副总裁。我是 Zynga 的总经理。我是通过一家初创公司到达那里的，当时我是一名工程师，最初是一名工程师，几年后担任产品主管，然后被 Zynga 收购，实际上，我在皮克斯动画工作室工作了近七年，开始了我的职业生涯，致力于视觉效果、软件工具和其他创意技术，尝试解决你可能看过或你的孩子看过的一系列精彩电影的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please tell us the films that you worked at. I had no idea that you worked at Pixar.
turns.zh: 请告诉我们您参与过的电影。我不知道你在皮克斯工作。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: I am credited on Finding Nemo, Cars, Wally, and Up.
turns.zh: 我的作品包括《海底总动员》、《汽车总动员》、《沃利》和《飞屋环游记》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What? I did not know any of this.
turns.zh: 什么？我对此一无所知。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Basically, I started there right out of college. I was super interested in computer graphics. I'd actually been an intern there, was very lucky to be interested in that in the moment where they were really accelerating the growth of the company going from like the whole company is working on one film to like, "Okay. We're trying to release a film every 18 months." So they really scaled up, and I had been studying computer graphics, and then I was an engineer focused on computer graphics and a little bit of research on that in college, was an intern there, and joined, and just got to see a fun growth period at that company, and really, I think in a lot of ways is the root of why I love doing product management because everything I worked on was at the intersections of interesting creative problems, interesting technical problems, and interesting storytelling problems.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。基本上，我大学一毕业就开始了。我对计算机图形学非常感兴趣。事实上，我曾在那里实习过，很幸运能够对他们真正加速公司发展的那一刻感兴趣，从整个公司都在制作一部电影变成“好吧。我们正努力每 18 个月发行一部电影。”所以他们真的扩大了规模，我一直在学习计算机图形学，然后我是一名专注于计算机图形学的工程师，并在大学里进行了一些研究，在那里实习，然后加入了，刚刚看到了那家公司的有趣的成长时期，真的，我认为在很多方面都是我喜欢做产品管理的根源，因为我所做的一切都是有趣的创意问题、有趣的技术问题和有趣的讲故事问题的交叉点。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So, in a lot of ways, it was like... I think if I connect the dots backwards to the Steve Jobsism is the beginning of how I got interested in solving high-level strategic problems across a bunch of different people doing different kinds of work and maybe how I got relatively good at it. It was because even as an engineer, I was sitting in the middle of those pieces, but I got bored, which sounds crazy, and decided to jump into a startup that nobody had ever heard of that had eight employees in 2006, and the rest is history from there.
turns.zh: 所以，在很多方面，这就像……我想，如果我把这些点与史蒂夫·乔布斯主义联系起来，那就是我对解决一群从事不同工作的不同人的高层战略问题产生兴趣的开始，也许我是如何变得相对擅长的。这是因为即使作为一名工程师，我也坐在这些碎片的中间，但我感到无聊，这听起来很疯狂，于是决定跳入一家没人听说过的初创公司，2006 年它有 8 名员工，剩下的就是从那里开始的历史。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I wasn't planning to talk about Pixar, but I am so curious. One more question there. What's something that you learned from Pixar that has informed the way that you build products or think about product or your career?
turns.zh: 是的。我本来不打算谈论皮克斯，但我很好奇。还有一个问题。您从皮克斯学到的哪些东西影响了您构建产品或思考产品或职业的方式？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: At the foundation of it is when I first got there, I thought what was important was modeling how things work in the real world. They're making things look right, so to speak. What I learned there is that actually, you're trying to deliver an end experience, and product, and story to your viewers, to your audience. It doesn't actually matter what's real. It matters what you see on the screen. It matters the emotion that it creates, the story that it creates, how it reinforces all of the other pieces. So the technical pieces were just a means to that end. So, of course, we used real physics and real math behind the scenes to do stuff, but if you had to box the numbers to make it look right, that's the right thing to do.
turns.zh: 当我第一次到达那里时，我认为重要的是模拟现实世界中事物的运作方式。可以这么说，他们正在让事情看起来正确。我从中了解到，实际上，您正在尝试向观众、观众提供最终体验、产品和故事。实际上什么是真实的并不重要。您在屏幕上看到的内容很重要。重要的是它所创造的情感、它所创造的故事以及它如何强化所有其他作品。所以技术部分只是达到这个目的的一种手段。所以，当然，我们在幕后使用了真实的物理和真实的数学来做事情，但如果你必须将数字装箱以使其看起来正确，那就是正确的做法。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So I remember as I was working on early effects, bubbles, sand, so this kind of stuff, I was trying to do things the way it would really work, and then the camel would look at it, and almost the first lesson I learned there was like, "No. What matters is the end result, the end product, the end feeling." I feel like I go back to that a lot as I think about product development not just from an engineering and technical standpoint, but from what's in your strategy doc isn't that important. It's actually just an input into the end experience that you're trying to deliver for customers. When we're thinking about content development in our programs, it's not important that all of the principles fit perfectly together into this MEC framework. It matters that you help people solve actual problems. What's the end goal that you're looking for? I feel like that's the lesson that I just keep going back to for my time there.
turns.zh: 所以我记得当我在研究早期效果，气泡，沙子，所以这类东西时，我试图以真正有效的方式做事，然后骆驼会看着它，我在那里学到的第一课几乎是，“不。重要的是最终结果，最终产品，最终感觉。”我觉得我经常回顾这一点，因为我不仅从工程和技术的角度思考产品开发，而且从战略文档中的内容来看也并不那么重要。它实际上只是您试图为客户提供的最终体验的输入。当我们考虑项目中的内容开发时，所有原则是否完美契合此 MEC 框架并不重要。帮助人们解决实际问题很重要。您正在寻找的最终目标是什么？我觉得这就是我在那里的那段时间不断回顾的教训。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a great segue to Reforge, which I want to spend a little bit of time on. Folks that listen to this podcast know that I'm a huge fan, and we have a lot of Reforge alumni on this podcast.
turns.zh: 这是重铸的一个很好的延续，我想花一点时间在上面。听这个播客的人都知道我是一个超级粉丝，而且这个播客上有很多 Reforge 校友。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So a couple questions there. One, you said you're a chief development officer. Is that your title?
turns.zh: 有几个问题。第一，你说你是首席开发官。这是你的头衔吗？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is it that you do as a chief development officer?
turns.zh: 作为首席开发官，您的职责是什么？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: It's funny because in a lot of ways, it's not a made-up title, but trying to figure out how a role that I ended up sliding into as I grew my engagement with the company, how do we describe what it is? So I think what's unique about Reforge versus a traditional software startup, or a SaaS company, or all the other things you see is that we're not just a software company. Of course, we have a website. Go to it. You see things, you deliberate, but we also build a lot of stuff and experiences that fit into that. We build content. We build programs today. We're going to build all kinds of other content. We have live cohort experiences that are designed and thoughtful, and we build and try to make, solve certain customer problems.
turns.zh: 这很有趣，因为从很多方面来说，这不是一个虚构的标题，而是试图弄清楚随着我与公司的接触不断加深，我最终是如何滑入这个角色的，我们如何描述它是什么？因此，我认为与传统软件初创公司、SaaS 公司或您看到的所有其他公司相比，Reforge 的独特之处在于我们不仅仅是一家软件公司。当然，我们有一个网站。去吧。你会看到事物，你会深思熟虑，但我们也构建了很多与之相适应的东西和体验。我们构建内容。我们今天构建程序。我们将构建各种其他内容。我们拥有经过设计和深思熟虑的现场队列体验，我们构建并尝试解决某些客户问题。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: We have a member slack that we try to design to solve certain problems. We have the people like yourself and a lot of the guests that you've had on the podcast like Elena, or Adam Fishman, or Casey who plugged into our system to help us build all of those things because at the end of the day, our job is to help unlock the expertise that's locked in the heads of the greatest operators in the world. So who do we work with? How do we develop that content? How do we make their ideas shine? How do we solve real member problems? How do we help people do work?
turns.zh: 我们有一个成员松弛，我们试图设计它来解决某些问题。我们有像您这样的人，还有很多像 Elena、Adam Fishman 或 Casey 这样的播客嘉宾，他们接入我们的系统来帮助我们构建所有这些东西，因为归根结底，我们的工作是帮助解锁世界上最伟大的操作员头脑中的专业知识。那么我们和谁一起工作呢？我们如何开发这些内容？我们如何让他们的想法闪闪发光？如何解决会员的实际问题？我们如何帮助人们工作？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: A lot of that is a product experience that in some ways, like a Pixar movie, there's the technical aspects and the UX aspects, but there's also all of the content, and the partners that we work with, and those pieces. I own all of that piece, like the production, content, the new product experiences, and all of the pieces that fit in there. So we have a team of really talented, amazing people that work on these things, and I lead those teams.
turns.zh: 其中很大一部分是产品体验，在某些方面，就像皮克斯电影一样，有技术方面和用户体验方面，但也有所有内容、与我们合作的合作伙伴以及这些片段。我拥有这一切，比如制作、内容、新产品体验以及所有适合其中的部分。因此，我们拥有一支由非常有才华、出色的人员组成的团队致力于这些事情，而我领导着这些团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how that comes back to your Pixar experience of the combination of intersection of art and technology.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这又回到了艺术与技术相结合的皮克斯体验。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so interesting. Okay. Never thought about it that way. Yeah.
turns.zh: 那太有趣了。好的。从来没有这样想过。是的。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Like we said, it's easier to connect the dots in reverse than moving forward. I have always been not that precious about titles, career roles, et cetera. I've really found myself drawn to, "Is this an interesting problem that I believe I can bring something valuable to the table? Can I help solve this in some meaningful way, and will I learn something great and new from this role?" At every step, I made those decisions. I've gone up and down the title stack from VP down to ICPM, from engineer to product, from product to this new thing and content. In every single one, I think it's a lot about, "What are you bringing to the table to help solve that problem? What are you taking away from the job and learning from it, and how do you turn that into the next step?"
turns.zh: 就像我们说的，将这些点反向连接起来比向前推进更容易。我一直不太重视头衔、职业角色等等。我真的发现自己很感兴趣，“这是一个有趣的问题吗？我相信我可以带来一些有价值的东西吗？我能以某种有意义的方式帮助解决这个问题吗？我会从这个角色中学到一些很棒的新东西吗？”在每一步中，我都做出了这些决定。我把头衔从 VP 到 ICPM，从工程师到产品，从产品到新事物和内容。我认为在每一个问题中，都有很多关于“你会带来什么来帮助解决这个问题？你从工作中学到了什么并从中学习到什么，以及你如何将其转化为下一步？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, and we're going to chat about a lot of those learnings from your experience going through these career journeys, but one last question on Reforge. Just like how big is Reforge at this point? How many cohorts? How many students? How many people work there? What's the operation scale at this point?
turns.zh: 太棒了，我们将讨论您从这些职业生涯中学到的很多东西，但最后一个问题是关于 Reforge 的。就像Reforge现在有多大？有多少个队列？有多少学生？有多少人在那里工作？目前运营规模是多少？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: It's hard to count how many employees because it's growing so fast. I believe we are at just around 150 total employees across the whole company right now.
turns.zh: 很难统计有多少员工，因为它增长得太快了。我相信目前整个公司的员工总数约为 150 人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: That doesn't include our executives and residents, subject matter experts, and the partners we work with. That's full-time employees working on the business. Of course, we have a large product development, product design, engineering, and data teams, but also the teams that I run. We call them strategy leads, content producers, content strategists, content designers, building all of that content as well as our partners team and operations team. So it's a relatively large company at this point. When I first started working with it, it was a scrappy operation of just a handful of folks, but we've grown quite a bit of over the last year.
turns.zh: 这不包括我们的高管和住院医生、主题专家以及与我们合作的合作伙伴。这是从事该业务的全职员工。当然，我们有庞大的产品开发、产品设计、工程和数据团队，还有我管理的团队。我们称他们为战略主管、内容制作人、内容战略家、内容设计师、构建所有这些内容以及我们的合作伙伴团队和运营团队。所以目前它是一家相对较大的公司。当我第一次开始使用它时，这是一个只有少数人的斗志旺盛的运作，但我们在去年已经成长了很多。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: With that, we support, I believe, now 19 total cohort-based programs across product, engineering, marketing, and growth-related topics as well as a bunch of new experiences that we're working on for the coming future here in the next year. We have well over 10,000 active members on the platform, about a dozen executives and residents that work to help us deliver those programs, and hundreds of partners. We call them experts and operators in the space who contribute to our programs in different ways either as guests or as mentors, or helping us develop content behind the scenes.
turns.zh: 我相信，有了这些，我们现在支持 19 个基于队列的项目，涵盖产品、工程、营销和增长相关主题，以及我们正在为明年的未来开发的一系列新体验。我们的平台上拥有超过 10,000 名活跃会员、大约十几名致力于帮助我们实施这些计划的高管和居民，以及数百名合作伙伴。我们称他们为该领域的专家和运营商，他们以不同的方式为我们的项目做出贡献，无论是作为嘉宾还是导师，或者帮助我们在幕后开发内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, and I taught a couple guest lectures this past cohort. I think my second ever lesson was with you. You were the teacher?
turns.zh: 太棒了，我在过去的队列中教授了几场客座讲座。我想我的第二堂课就是和你一起上的。你是老师吗？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yes. Yeah. We talked about instant buy, I think they're called, but I can't remember the name.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。我们谈到了即时购买，我想他们被称为，但我不记得名字了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Instant book. Close, close.
turns.zh: 即时预订。关闭，关闭。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Instant book, sorry.
turns.zh: 即时预订，抱歉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: On the Reforge platform for experimentation and testing program, which was, yeah, actually, also my first program that I helped lead at Reforge, and I think you were my first guest.
turns.zh: 在 Reforge 平台上进行实验和测试项目，是的，实际上，这也是我在 Reforge 帮助领导的第一个项目，我想你是我的第一位客人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my god.
turns.zh: 我的天啊。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So, thanks. Thanks for not making me look bad.
turns.zh: 所以，谢谢。谢谢你没有让我难堪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you. So what's cool about your background working at Reforge and all the companies you worked at is that you've seen a lot of PM careers go well and PM careers go not so well. So what I want to spend our time on is talking through just the career development journey for product managers and in particular, the challenges that PMs face trying to become better PMs and just why it's innately tricky to become better as a product manager. It's such a weird job to get better at. So my first question is actually, why is it so hard to become better as a PM? Why is it innately a tricky thing to develop as a PM?
turns.zh: 谢谢。因此，您在 Reforge 以及您工作过的所有公司的工作背景的一个很酷的地方是，您看到很多 PM 职业发展顺利，但 PM 职业发展不太顺利。因此，我想花时间谈谈产品经理的职业发展历程，特别是产品经理在努力成为更好的产品经理时所面临的挑战，以及为什么成为更好的产品经理天生就很棘手。这是一项很奇怪的工作，需要做得更好。所以我的第一个问题实际上是，为什么成为一名更好的产品经理这么难？为什么成为一名 PM 天生就是一件棘手的事情？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: One of the trickiest bits about it is that there's no clear, obvious pre-training you can do that gives you a baseline set of understanding that you can use to be a product manager. People come from MBAs, people come from certain kinds of majors in college, et cetera, but it's not engineering where like, "Okay. With a couple of weeks of bootcamp or a couple of years of a computer science education, I have some foundational knowledge that helps me go from zero to one in my first job." Not only does it help me break in because I have a credential that helps me land that job, and we can talk about why landing your first PM job is so hard, but also, there's not a lot of stuff that one-to-one directly correlates to the work you're going do on a day-to-day basis.
turns.zh: 最棘手的一点是，你没有可以做的清晰、明显的预培训来为你提供一套可以用来成为产品经理的基本理解。人们来自 MBA，人们来自大学的某些专业，等等，但这不是工程学，“好吧。通过几周的训练营或几年的计算机科学教育，我掌握了一些基础知识，可以帮助我在第一份工作中从零到一。”它不仅可以帮助我融入进来，因为我拥有可以帮助我找到这份工作的证书，而且我们可以讨论为什么找到你的第一份 PM 工作如此困难，而且，没有很多东西与你日常要做的工作一对一直接相关。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: I think there's an idea that Naval Ravikant talked about on Twitter and in blog posts a long time ago, this concept of specific knowledge that can only be gathered by actually doing the work. A lot of product management, really, is like that. You get better by doing it, and so you start in the same place, if that makes sense. Of course, there are different skills and intellectual capacities, et cetera that help different people be more successful at it, but at the end of the day, you don't know if a PM is going to be great until they start doing that work. So I think that's one of the pieces that's very hard.
turns.zh: 我认为 Naval Ravikant 很久以前在 Twitter 和博客文章中谈到了一个想法，即只有通过实际工作才能收集的特定知识的概念。事实上，很多产品管理都是这样的。通过这样做你会变得更好，所以你从同一个地方开始，如果这有意义的话。当然，有不同的技能和智力等可以帮助不同的人在这方面取得更大的成功，但最终，在他们开始做这项工作之前，你不知道 PM 是否会很棒。所以我认为这是非常困难的部分之一。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: The second is the thing I just alluded to, which is breaking in and getting your first role. It's just a very difficult situation for a lot of companies, and there are a couple of different paths to it, but none of them are straightforward. There's no clear linear path, except for maybe being a Stanford or Harvard grad, top-tier school grad, NCS with an internship, goes to Google to do an APM program. There are a couple of these things that are surefire, but I don't think they guarantee success, and they are actually very limited in terms of the number of people that they let into the business.
turns.zh: 第二个就是我刚才提到的，就是闯入并获得你的第一个角色。对于很多公司来说，这是一个非常困难的局面，有几种不同的路径可以实现，但没有一条是直截了当的。没有明确的线性路径，除了可能是斯坦福大学或哈佛大学的毕业生、顶尖学校的毕业生、NCS 实习生、去 Google 做 APM 项目。其中有一些事情是肯定会成功的，但我认为它们并不能保证成功，而且就其允许进入该行业的人数而言，它们实际上非常有限。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So I think this is what makes it so hard is that there's not any upfront training you can really do to prepare yourself or even knock down the door to break in. But then, also, it's not clear there's a lot of training within a company that would help you be successful generally on the job of product management. You can learn how to be a good PM at Google, you can learn to be a good PM at Facebook, but it is up to each individual PM to figure out how to generalize what they're doing to move from different kinds of product across different kinds of product work as they get more senior to solve bigger problems, et cetera.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，这就是它如此困难的原因，因为你没有任何真正可以做的前期培训来让自己做好准备，甚至敲门进入。但同时，也不清楚公司内部是否有很多培训可以帮助你在产品管理工作上取得成功。你可以学习如何在 Google 成为一名优秀的 PM，你可以学习如何在 Facebook 成为一名优秀的 PM，但是每个 PM 都需要弄清楚如何概括他们正在做的事情，以便随着他们的级别越来越高来解决更大的问题，从不同类型的产品转向不同类型的产品工作，等等。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So what we tried to do at Reforge is we are focused on helping people accelerate that learning loop. It's not, "Hey, if you take this class, now you're qualified to be a PM." It's not really like that. I don't know if that's possible. I hope it will be someday, but it is very difficult. I think it's more, "Hey, we want to help you when you encounter certain kinds of problems, not have to solve them from first principles, but following the footsteps of the people who have done great work in the past, generalize those lessons." But at the end of the day, you still have to get down and do the work.
turns.zh: 因此，我们在 Reforge 所做的就是专注于帮助人们加速学习循环。这并不是说，“嘿，如果你参加了这门课程，现在你就有资格成为一名产品经理了。”事实并非如此。我不知道这是否可能。我希望有一天会实现，但这非常困难。我认为更多的是，“嘿，当你遇到某些类型的问题时，我们想帮助你，不必从第一原则来解决它们，而是追随过去做出伟大工作的人们的脚步，总结那些经验教训。”但归根结底，你还是得坐下来做工作。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: You can't do homework, you can't do exercises, you can't do fake stuff. You have to work on real products at real companies with real customers, with real data to get better at product management. So any kind of training, mentorship, reading, et cetera that you do is just a layer on top of that. The real acceleration happens from doing it and getting more reps. There are ways that I think great PMs use to go faster on this loop, but you still have to do the work. At the core is you have to actually execute and deliver great products, and you have to do it over, and over, and over again.
turns.zh: 你不能做作业，你不能做练习，你不能做假事情。你必须在真实的​​公司、真实的客户、真实的数据上开发真实的产品，才能更好地进行产品管理。因此，你所做的任何类型的培训、指导、阅读等都只是在此之上的一层。真正的加速来自于做这件事并获得更多次数。我认为优秀的产品经理可以使用一些方法来加快这个循环，但你仍然需要完成工作。核心是你必须实际执行和交付出色的产品，并且你必须一遍又一遍地这样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes. Let's absolutely dig into that. Let me put out a couple mental models that I'm thinking as you're talking.
turns.zh: 是的。让我们深入探讨一下。让我列出一些在你说话时我正在思考的心理模型。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One is just if you think about a pie chart of a great PM's career and/or investments they make along their career journey, how do you break up that pie chart? Like some percentage is doing the work, some percentage is courses, maybe some percentage is books. So just putting that out there in case that's useful to think about, and then the other is thinking about the trajectory of a PM on a line chart, and what are these inflection points that you've seen most impact the career trajectory of a PM?
turns.zh: 一个问题是，如果你想一下一位优秀产品经理的职业生涯和/或他们在职业生涯中所做的投资的饼图，你如何分解这个饼图？就像一部分人在做工作，一部分人在做课程，一部分人可能在做书本。因此，只需将其放在那里，以防万一思考有用，然后另一个是在折线图上思考 PM 的轨迹，以及您所看到的对 PM 职业轨迹影响最大的这些拐点是什么？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So let's start at the first one, the pie chart idea. What percent is spent on different things? Unsurprisingly because Reforge is all about growth loops, I think of this in terms of a loop actually, which is like, "What is that learning or career acceleration, or ability acceleration loop? At the core, again, at the top of the loop is execution. You have to have a real problem. You're working on with real customers that you want to solve in some way. So, you're executing. You're delivering. You're learning at the beginning. It's all about execution. So we'll start with the pie chart at the beginning. It's almost all execution.
turns.zh: 让我们从第一个开始，饼图的想法。在不同的事情上花费了多少百分比？毫不奇怪，因为 Reforge 都是关于增长循环的，所以我实际上从循环的角度来考虑这一点，就像是，“什么是学习或职业加速，或能力加速循环？核心，再说一次，循环的顶部是执行。你必须有一个真正的问题。你正在与你想要以某种方式解决的真正客户一起工作。所以，你正在执行。你正在交付。你从一开始就在学习。这都是关于执行的。所以我们将从一开始的饼图开始，几乎都是执行。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: What are the problems you give a junior or brand new PM? Known problem, known solution. "Please work with engineering and design to deliver that thing on time, and then tell us what happened." So it's like a very tightly constrained problem. As you level up, then some of these things become more unknowns. So there's execution, but I think the next step that great product managers do is they think about how to generalize that execution a little bit. So it's not just, "Okay. Now, I know what the best settings page for Slack is." It's, "What generalizations did you make? What are the things that you can take that are applicable to other stuff?"
turns.zh: 您给初级或全新的 PM 提出了哪些问题？已知问题，已知解决方案。 “请与工程和设计部门合作，按时交付该产品，然后告诉我们发生了什么。”所以这就像一个非常严格约束的问题。当你升级时，其中一些事情会变得更加未知。所以有执行力，但我认为优秀的产品经理下一步要做的是考虑如何概括执行力。所以这不仅仅是“好吧。现在，我知道 Slack 的最佳设置页面是什么。”它是，“你做了什么概括？你可以采取哪些适用于其他事物的东西？”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Some of that is execution-oriented, how to best work with engineers, how to iterate on designs, what customers do and don't do, rules of thumb, those kinds of things. I think that's where reading courses, et cetera can help because sometimes by bringing other... or one-on-one conversations with experts, et cetera. There are a whole bunch of different ways, but is that the generalization step? "Hey, I did this thing. Oh, other people have done something similar. How do I connect the dots on that? How do I make this experience bigger than what I've just done and lead me to help solve other problems?"
turns.zh: 其中一些是面向执行的，如何最好地与工程师合作，如何迭代设计，客户做什么和不做什么，经验法则，诸如此类的事情。我认为这就是阅读课程等可以提供帮助的地方，因为有时可以通过其他……或与专家的一对一对话等方式。有很多不同的方法，但这就是泛化步骤吗？ “嘿，我做了这件事。哦，其他人也做了类似的事情。我如何将这些点联系起来？我如何使这个经历比我刚刚所做的更重要，并引导我帮助解决其他问题？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These are things you're doing in your head, basically. You're just developing frameworks, mental models, things that you're just taking with you to the next project in your mind.
turns.zh: 基本上，这些都是你在脑子里做的事情。你只是在开发框架、心智模型，以及你只是将其带到你脑海中的下一个项目中的东西。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Exactly. So, to use an example, there was a time at Instacart where we were working on onboarding, brand new onboarding and activation flow for customers. We tried a lot of different stuff. We tried the slimmest, fastest, lowest friction, least number of steps path in, and then we had this hypothesis about helping people get set up. So we took the opposite approach, which was a really long onboarding with a bunch of different steps and wanted to see, "Was that more effective or less effective?"
turns.zh: 确切地。举个例子，有一段时间，我们在 Instacart 致力于为客户提供引导、全新的引导和激活流程。我们尝试了很多不同的东西。我们尝试了最纤细、最快、摩擦最小、步数最少的路径，然后我们有了帮助人们入门的假设。因此，我们采取了相反的方法，这是一个非常漫长的入职过程，包含一系列不同的步骤，并想看看“这是否更有效或更不有效？”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: The generalization is, "Oh, for products that had a high bar to activation, sometimes more set up and higher friction, good friction could actually help those customers be successful. There are other kinds of products that are high-intent where they know what they need to do to have simple actions where lowering friction might be the right thing." So, that's a generalization. It's a generalization of, "Oh, I learned a thing." It's a hypothesis about how that might generalize other kinds of products or other kinds of problems that you approach. I think some of that can come from seeing it from the outside, listening to a podcast, hearing you say it, taking a course, et cetera. But at the end of the day, you have to experience it to see how it applies to the world.
turns.zh: 概括来说，“哦，对于激活门槛较高的产品，有时需要更多的设置和更高的摩擦力，良好的摩擦力实际上可以帮助这些客户取得成功。还有其他类型的产品是高意图的，他们知道需要做什么才能采取简单的行动，而降低摩擦力可能是正确的事情。”所以，这是一个概括。这是“哦，我学到了一件事”的概括。这是一个关于如何推广其他类型的产品或您处理的其他类型的问题的假设。我认为其中一些可以来自于从外部看到它、听播客、听你说、参加课程等等。但最终，你必须体验它才能了解它如何应用于世界。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Then, the next bit is communication, and I think this is a bit that a lot of product managers, obviously, and any job miss, but you can't just do the work. You have to actually communicate the work. You have to talk about what you're doing, what you've generalized, what you've learned so that you can hit the next step, which is scale your opportunities. Go from smaller known problem, known solution to maybe known problem, unknown solution type of work, which is the next step.
turns.zh: 然后，下一点是沟通，我认为这是很多产品经理显然和任何工作都会错过的一点，但你不能只做工作。你必须实际交流工作。你必须谈论你正在做的事情、你归纳的内容、你学到的东西，这样你才能进行下一步，即扩大你的机会。从较小的已知问题、已知解决方案到可能已知问题、未知解决方案类型的工作，这是下一步。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Then, eventually, to where you want to be as a senior, great, high-level individual contributor PM to the not quite known problem, maybe a goal with a set of problems and unknown solutions, unknown problems, unknown solutions, where you're actually identifying customer problems and moving towards on that. So scaling up your opportunity, and then executing again. I think of this as a loop of learning, and so of course, the percentages change over time as you move more senior in your career, but also, depending on where you're at in the step that the percentages change.
turns.zh: 然后，最终，你想成为一名高级、伟大、高水平的个人贡献者 PM，解决不太为人所知的问题，也许是一个包含一系列问题和未知解决方案、未知问题、未知解决方案的目标，你实际上是在识别客户问题并朝着这个目标迈进。因此，扩大你的机会，然后再次执行。我认为这是一个学习循环，所以当然，随着你在职业生涯中晋升，百分比会随着时间的推移而变化，但也取决于你在百分比变化的步骤中所处的位置。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So, just to recap, execute, just do the work, just ship.
turns.zh: 知道了。所以，回顾一下，执行，完成工作，交付。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Generalize learnings from shipping to build up your gut feeling of what will work and not work.
turns.zh: 总结从运输中学到的知识，建立自己的直觉，判断什么是有效的，什么是无效的。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Learn to communicate things you're doing, and then scale the things that you're executing based on this gut feeling you're building, and communicate that out, and just continue. Do you think scaling take on more scope or have more impact? Is that how you think about scaling, that last piece?
turns.zh: 学会沟通你正在做的事情，然后根据你正在建立的直觉来扩展你正在执行的事情，并将其传达出来，然后继续。您认为规模扩大会带来更大的范围还是产生更大的影响？这就是你对最后一块缩放的看法吗？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah. I think it's one moving from knowns to unknowns.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为这是从已知走向未知的过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 伟大的。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So like you're being given a hairier, harder to untangle types of problems with more unknowns and more autonomy. I think the second is, yeah, of course, with... although I think for the beginning of your career, you tend to go deeper. So it's like, "Okay. I'm going to work on growth, let's say, or core product, or zero-to-one products, or technical scaling, whatever it is. I'm going to go deeper on that," and then over time, that turns into width, but this is why the generalization step is important.
turns.zh: 就像你被赋予了一个更棘手、更难解决的问题，更多的未知数和更多的自主权。我认为第二个是，是的，当然，......虽然我认为在你职业生涯的开始，你往往会走得更深。所以这就像是，“好吧。我将致力于增长，比如说，核心产品，或零到一产品，或技术扩展，无论是什么。我将更深入地研究它，”然后随着时间的推移，它会变成宽度，但这就是为什么泛化步骤很重要。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: If you want to be a product leader, you cannot be seen solely as a specialist in that certain kind of product work, and so the generalization step is really important. If you want to move from growth to core product, you need to show that you're not just running experiments and driving numbers up. You need to show and communicate that you're learning deeper lessons about how customer psychology works, and what products people resonate with, and how to think about the business more holistically, and then communication. No one knows what you're thinking if you don't tell them. So if you don't communicate, you don't have control over those scaled opportunities. Usually, your manager, or the organization, or the company does. Maybe by switching jobs, you have some control, but you need to earn that right. You need to communicate. That's why I think there's pieces of the loop you can control and pieces that are externalized.
turns.zh: 如果你想成为一名产品领导者，你不能仅仅被视为某类产品工作的专家，因此泛化步骤非常重要。如果你想从增长转向核心产品，你需要表明你不仅仅是进行实验和推动数字上升。您需要表明并传达您正在学习更深入的课程，例如客户心理如何发挥作用，人们会对哪些产品产生共鸣，以及如何更全面地思考业务，然后进行沟通。如果你不告诉他们，没有人知道你在想什么。因此，如果你不沟通，你就无法控制这些规模化的机会。通常，您的经理、组织或公司会这样做。也许通过换工作，你可以拥有一定的控制权，但你需要赢得这种权利。你们需要沟通。这就是为什么我认为循环的某些部分是您可以控制的，而有些部分是外部化的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious, in your own career, what the biggest inflections of growth have been either in terms of learning, or impact, or just opportunity?
turns.zh: 我很好奇，在您自己的职业生涯中，最大的成长变化是在学习、影响还是机会方面？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: The first big one was when I switched from being an engineer to being a product... I didn't even know it was product management, but a product leader of some kind. I think there are two things that happen. One is you got to be doing this stuff, but often, somebody needs to see it. The scale opportunity piece of the step often requires someone from outside to notice that you're doing something really well and trust you with a bigger opportunity. I think of this as sponsorship, not mentorship. I don't necessarily find that in my career. I've had a lot of managers where I'm like, "Wow, their day-to-day help was super awesome at helping me be a better leader."
turns.zh: 第一个重大事件是当我从工程师转向产品时……我什至不知道这是产品管理，而是某种产品负责人。我认为发生了两件事。一是你必须做这些事情，但通常，需要有人看到它。该步骤中的扩大机会部分通常需要外部人员注意到您在某件事上做得非常好，并相信您会获得更大的机会。我认为这是赞助，而不是指导。在我的职业生涯中我不一定会发现这一点。我遇到过很多经理，我会说：“哇，他们的日常帮助非常出色，帮助我成为一名更好的领导者。”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: I hope that I've been that for some people, but I don't have a ton of examples of that in my career. But what I do have is a couple examples of people who deeply trusted me to solve big problems, and I don't know. I'm lucky to have had that or otherwise, but one was a CEO of that startup who's now a venture capitalist. His name is Nabeel Hyatt. I was like, "Hey, you seem to understand the data better than anybody here. You're solving these problems. Help us figure out what we're going to do next," which now we call product management.
turns.zh: 我希望我对某些人来说也是这样，但在我的职业生涯中并没有很多这样的例子。但我确实有几个例子，他们深信我能解决大问题，但我不知道。我很幸运有过这样的经历或其他经历，但其中一位是那家初创公司的首席执行官，现在是一名风险投资家。他的名字叫纳比尔·海厄特。我当时想，“嘿，你似乎比这里的任何人都更了解数据。你正在解决这些问题。帮助我们弄清楚下一步要做什么”，现在我们称之为产品管理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But he was at, by the way?
turns.zh: 但顺便说一句，他当时在吗？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: it was called Conduit Labs.
turns.zh: 它被称为管道实验室。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的。是的。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: It's a game company. Then, eventually, I was the director of product for our Boston studio. The next was at Slack. I was an ICPM working on activation and growth on a team of three or four other PMs, and there were a couple of moments where by communicating my work and talking through how I was solving problems, people noticed that I knew what I was doing and gave me bigger and bigger opportunities. One of those was Merci Grace, who I think has been on your pod and was a wonderful sponsor for me. Then, again, when Merci left, April Underwood, who's the CPO, said, "It seems like you have a handle on this. I'd like you to take on a bigger range of problems across all of this growth and not just the modernization piece that I've been working on before." So I think in each of those steps it's about creating trust and knowing that you have a sponsor there, someone who's going to go to bat for you.
turns.zh: 这是一家游戏公司。然后，最终，我成为了我们波士顿工作室的产品总监。下一个是在 Slack。我是一名 ICPM，在一个由三四个其他 PM 组成的团队中负责激活和成长，有几次，通过交流我的工作并谈论我如何解决问题，人们注意到我知道自己在做什么，并给了我越来越大的机会。其中之一是 Merci Grace，我想他一直在你的 Pod 中，并且对我来说是一个很棒的赞助商。然后，当 Merci 离开时，首席产品官艾普丽尔·安德伍德 (April Underwood) 说道：“看来你已经掌握了这个问题。我希望你能解决整个增长过程中更广泛的问题，而不仅仅是我之前一直在处理的现代化问题。”所以我认为在每一个步骤中，都是为了建立信任，并知道你有一个赞助商，一个会为你奋斗的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really love this point of sponsorship. We haven't talked a lot about this on the podcast. There's a lot of talk of finding a coach or having a manager that teaches you how to do the job, but this idea of just getting to a place where someone gives you an opportunity to shine, and that's been really big in my career just like certain managers just, "Here, Lenny. You take this, and let's see what you can do."
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个赞助点。我们在播客上还没有对此进行太多讨论。很多人都在谈论寻找一位教练或一位经理来教你如何做这份工作，但这种想法就是去一个能让你有机会发光的地方，这在我的职业生涯中非常重要，就像某些经理一样，“在这里，莱尼。你拿着这个，让我们看看你能做什么。”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else you can recommend to folks to create opportunities for sponsorship? You talked about communication, executing well. Is that just the core of it, like doing a great job and communicating the great job you're doing?
turns.zh: 您还有什么可以推荐给人们来创造赞助机会的吗？你谈到了沟通和执行力。这只是它的核心吗，比如做好工作并传达你正在做的出色工作？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: This idea that it's what you do and that's multiplied by your ability to show that work and communicate it, and that's the impact that you can have, but you have to have not just impact on the customers, but also on the organization. I think it is impact on the organization, changing the way people think about problems, helping generalize what works and what doesn't work, bringing learnings to the table.
turns.zh: 这种想法是，这就是你所做的事情，乘以你展示工作和沟通工作的能力，这就是你可以产生的影响，但你不仅要对客户产生影响，还要对组织产生影响。我认为这对组织有影响，改变人们思考问题的方式，帮助总结什么有效，什么无效，将经验教训带到桌面上。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: For me, I've worked a lot on growth, and I've treated a huge part of my job as not just moving the numbers, but also teaching the organization how our growth model works, how the pieces fit together, what our customers care about, what's working, what's not working, and that creates a lot of, A, leverage in other parts of the organization because they can do better work by having more information, but also, B, trust. Trust from leadership, trust from your peers, and otherwise.
turns.zh: 对我来说，我在增长方面做了很多工作，我工作的很大一部分不仅仅是移动数字，而且还教导组织我们的增长模式如何运作，各部分如何组合在一起，我们的客户关心什么，什么有效，什么无效，这在组织的其他部分创造了很多，A，杠杆，因为他们可以通过拥有更多信息来更好地工作，而且，B，信任。来自领导的信任、来自同事的信任等等。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So, now, how do you get to that? Some of it is just luck. Someone has got to believe in you. You can create your luck by being good at communicating and solving hard problems. I think the other piece is knowing when you go into an organization, "Is this a role that's important to the company? Is it on the list?" I think it is easier to find sponsors, communicate, and create leverage if the thing you're working on is in the top four or five most important things the company is working on. I find myself drawn to those kinds of problems, and I think that's one way because then, all of a sudden, CEOs notice what you're working on, heads of product notice what you're working on, and your peers notice what you're working on.
turns.zh: 那么，现在，你如何做到这一点呢？其中一些只是运气。必须有人相信你。你可以通过善于沟通和解决难题来创造你的运气。我认为另一件事是当你进入一个组织时要知道，“这个角色对公司来说重要吗？它在名单上吗？”我认为，如果你正在做的事情是公司正在做的最重要的四到五个事情之一，那么找到赞助商、沟通和创造影响力会更容易。我发现自己被这类问题所吸引，我认为这是一种方式，因为突然之间，首席执行官注意到你在做什么，产品负责人注意到你在做什么，你的同事也注意到你在做什么。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: The other bit is curiosity. I think to be in the seat where people want to sponsor you, I think you have to show a handle on not just what you're doing, but how that relates to all of the things around you. So I call this going two stack levels up, two stack levels down in terms of your curiosity and what you understand, and also, knowing what's to the left and what's to the right. So let's use the example of if I'm working on activation on growth, let's say, or monetization. It doesn't matter. One of those two pieces. When I say two stack levels down, I like to understand how we build customers, how it works in Stripe, what are our dunning policies, what are the technical things that work and don't work in the pieces maybe down to the database. Right?
turns.zh: 另一点是好奇心。我认为，要想坐在人们想要赞助你的位置上，我认为你不仅要掌控自己正在做的事情，还要掌控它与你周围所有事物的关系。因此，根据您的好奇心和您的理解，以及了解左侧和右侧的内容，我将其称为向上两个堆栈级别，向下两个堆栈级别。因此，让我们以我正在致力于增长激活或货币化为例。没关系。这两块中的一块。当我说向下两个堆栈级别时，我喜欢了解我们如何建立客户，它在 Stripe 中如何工作，我们的催款政策是什么，哪些技术部分有效，哪些无效（可能具体到数据库）。正确的？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: It's like technical curiosity, those kinds of things, but also mental models for what's above you. How do we grow? How does modernization fit into that? What are the trade-offs versus free growth versus paid growth? How important is this to the company? How does it fit into our long-term strategy? Those kinds of things. So it's like the strategic things above you. I like two stack levels because it's like you should understand your boss's priorities and your boss's boss's priorities. Eventually, that means you have to know what the board is thinking, right? Then, left and right is, "What are the core product teams working on that I could help advise on in terms of modernization or they could advise me on what they're thinking and what might be coming next? How do we fit together with the enterprise part of the business even though I'm working on self-serve? How do I think about sales? Do they have input, like interesting customer conversations or input?
turns.zh: 这就像技术上的好奇心，诸如此类的事情，但也包括对你之上的事物的心理模型。我们如何成长？现代化如何融入其中？自由增长与付费增长之间的权衡是什么？这对公司有多重要？它如何适应我们的长期战略？诸如此类的事情。所以这就像你上面的战略性事情。我喜欢两个堆栈级别，因为这就像你应该了解你老板的优先事项和你老板的老板的优先事项。最终，这意味着你必须知道董事会的想法，对吗？然后，左边和右边是，“我可以在现代化方面提供建议的核心产品团队是什么，或者他们可以就他们的想法和接下来可能发生的事情向我提供建议？即使我从事自助服务，我们如何与业务的企业部分结合在一起？我如何看待销售？他们是否有意见，例如有趣的客户对话或意见？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: It's this curiosity like walking around, getting to know what people are doing, and being seen as an expert. Are you the desk people go to when they have questions? Are you a person that people ask the opinion when you're trying to figure out how the dots connect? I have found for me, maybe this is just because this is a strength of mine, that connecting the dots of how the whole company works and how all the pieces fit together has been one of the ways that I've driven that sponsorship. I think for each individual, you have to figure out what your superpower is and where you can be actually top 10%, and then lean into opportunities and also problems that help you show that and shine it that way.
turns.zh: 这种好奇心就像四处走动，了解人们在做什么，并被视为专家。当人们有问题时，你是他们的咨询台吗？当你试图弄清楚这些点之间的联系时，人们会向你征求意见吗？我发现，也许这只是因为这是我的强项，将整个公司如何运作以及所有各个部分如何组合在一起的各个点联系起来是我推动赞助的方式之一。我认为对于每个人来说，你都必须弄清楚你的超能力是什么，以及你在哪里可以真正成为前 10%，然后抓住机会和问题来帮助你展示这一能力并以这种方式发光。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such cool advice. I think what's cool about that is I imagine you just go to your manager and even just ask, "Hey, I'd love to understand just what are your highest priorities, and then what are your manager's?" Just ask these questions. Just that alone I think communicates a lot about how much you care and your interest there, and that creates trust, even if you don't do a ton with it, and knowing what your manager cares about is just going to help in so many other ways just like, "Okay. This matters to them. I'm going to make sure to do a good job there."
turns.zh: 这是非常酷的建议。我认为这很酷的是，我想你只要去找你的经理，甚至只是问，“嘿，我很想了解你的最高优先事项是什么，然后你的经理的优先事项是什么？”只要问这些问题就可以了。我认为仅此一点就可以传达出你对那里的关心程度和兴趣，这会产生信任，即使你没有做很多事情，并且了解你的经理关心什么只会在很多其他方面提供帮助，就像，“好吧。这对他们很重要。我将确保在那里做好工作。”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So that is a really cool framework.
turns.zh: 所以这是一个非常酷的框架。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Not only do a good job there, but I'm going to figure out how to communicate what I'm doing to be only the parts that are important and matter to them. I'm going to know that when I hit a certain decision that needs to be made, whether I need their input or not. There are all these different pieces like understanding when to be heads-down, when to be heads-up, when to communicate, when not to, but I think understanding how all the pieces fit together, you really just try, and I always think of it as trying to build a mental model of how the company works, and what's important to it, and what's the equation, so to speak, or what are all the boxes, and then figure out like, "How is my work creating leverage in that?" I find that when you are thinking at that level, people tend to trust you.
turns.zh: 不仅要做好工作，而且我还要弄清楚如何将我正在做的事情传达给他们，只做对他们来说重要且重要的部分。我会知道，当我做出某个需要做出的决定时，我是否需要他们的意见。有很多不同的部分，比如理解什么时候低头，什么时候抬头，什么时候沟通，什么时候不沟通，但我认为理解所有这些部分如何组合在一起，你真的只是尝试，我总是认为这是试图建立一个关于公司如何运作的心智模型，什么对公司重要，什么是等式，可以这么说，或者所有的盒子是什么，然后弄清楚，“我的工作如何在其中创造影响力？”我发现当你在这个层面上思考时，人们往往会信任你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The core of trust is people. Your manager and their leaders need to feel like you will do a good job and a bigger responsibility, and what gives them trust? Oh, they do a good job, or they're curious, and excited, and understand all these things that they need to understand. So it all makes sense, and I'm always weary of asking PMs to do more work. It's such a busy, long hours job already, and what's cool about these things you're talking about is it's not necessarily a lot more work. It's just a little bit of research and a little bit of digging and thinking.
turns.zh: 信任的核心是人。你的经理和他们的领导者需要感觉你会做好工作并承担更大的责任，什么给了他们信任？哦，他们做得很好，或者他们很好奇，很兴奋，并且理解所有这些他们需要理解的事情。所以这一切都是有道理的，而且我总是厌倦要求产品经理做更多的工作。这已经是一项忙碌、长时间的工作了，而你所谈论的这些事情的酷之处在于它不一定需要更多的工作。只是一点点研究，一点点挖掘和思考。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah. I think the hard part of this is I have not figured out how to do this well in a remote environment without throwing a lot of one-on-ones on people's calendars because sometimes you figured this out just by hearing conversations, hang out at lunch, and asking questions, and those kinds of things, but it's certainly not impossible. You just have to work out a little more,
turns.zh: 是的。我认为其中困难的部分是，我还没有弄清楚如何在远程环境中做好这件事，而不需要在人们的日历上投入大量一对一的时间，因为有时你只是通过听对话、在午餐时闲逛、提出问题以及诸如此类的事情来解决这个问题，但这当然不是不可能的。你只需要多锻炼一点

turns.en: Just more Zooms.
