turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I know something you spend a lot of time thinking about is the transition from an ICPM to a manager, and you have this really epic post that I think you call the Product Leader Canyon that you think of this as a canyon that a lot of PMs don't cross. So I want to spend a little bit of time here. Can you maybe just talk about what this canyon is, and why it exists?
turns.zh: 所以我知道你花了很多时间思考从 ICPM 到经理的转变，你有一个非常史诗般的职位，我认为你称之为产品领导者峡谷，你认为这是一个很多 PM 都不会跨越的峡谷。所以我想在这里花一点时间。您能否谈谈这个峡谷是什么以及它为何存在？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah. We talked a little bit about the first of very hard part in product management career development, which is like, "How do I land my first job?" Not a pro at that. We can talk about that more, but then this path from IC to more senior IC working on bigger problems that have more business impact, et cetera, it's a relatively straightforward path. We just talked about some of the ways that you do that. You get a deeper understanding across a wider range of business problems. You solve more unknowns versus being handed problems to solve, et cetera, and you do that by being good at your job. You do that by being good at your job basically as a solo product manager on an island.
turns.zh: 是的。我们讨论了产品管理职业发展中第一个非常困难的部分，就像“我如何找到第一份工作？”不是专业人士。我们可以对此进行更多讨论，但是从 IC 到更高级的 IC 的路径致力于解决具有更大业务影响的更大问题，等等，这是一条相对简单的路径。我们刚刚讨论了做到这一点的一些方法。您可以更深入地了解更广泛的业务问题。你解决了更多的未知数，而不是被交给要解决的问题等等，并且你通过擅长你的工作来做到这一点。你可以通过在岛上担任独立产品经理来做好自己的工作来做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: We talked about communication and those kinds of things, but at the end of the day, like we described, most of the work is execution. Most of the work is partnering with your engineering manager, partnering with your designer and your team to build stuff and deliver stuff. You've gotten there by being really good at that. Right? You've gotten there by getting in the weeds, getting in the details, sweating what matters, working hard at it. So someone says, "We'd love for you to lead this team." Great. It's really easy to look at that and say, "Okay. Now, instead of owning free to paid conversion, I own growth overall."
turns.zh: 我们讨论了沟通之类的事情，但最终，正如我们所描述的，大部分工作都是执行。大部分工作是与您的工程经理合作，与您的设计师和团队合作来构建和交付内容。你已经做到了这一点，因为你真的很擅长这一点。正确的？你是通过深入了解、关注细节、专注于重要的事情、努力工作来实现这一目标的。于是有人说：“我们希望你能领导这个团队。”伟大的。很容易看到这一点并说：“好吧。现在，我不再拥有免费到付费的转化，而是拥有整体增长。”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: The first thing you do is start to figure out, "What are the most interesting and valuable projects that I can work on? As an IC, I can only have one person on my team to go dive in and work on those things to make a lot of leverage." This can create a little bit of a spiral of failure because it's the hard job. The IC part of the job is really hard. So, now, I gave you more work across more things, and you're already working 56 hours a week. Now, you got to keep track of more projects across more teams and more people, and maybe you kept the two or three most critical ones to yourself.
turns.zh: 你要做的第一件事就是开始弄清楚，“我能从事的最有趣、最有价值的项目是什么？作为一名 IC，我的团队中只能有一个人深入研究这些事情，才能发挥很大的作用。”这可能会导致失败，因为这是一项艰巨的工作。 IC部分的工作确实很辛苦。所以，现在，我给了你更多的工作，涉及更多的事情，而你已经每周工作 56 小时。现在，您必须跟踪更多团队和更多人员的更多项目，并且也许您将两三个最关键的项目留给自己。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So that's one angle is learning about, yes, it's probably the right thing in the near term for you to focus, and work on this, and be really directive about what to do, and get in every single detail, and make sure you deliver the best product. But long run, you've taken a learning opportunity away from someone else, and you've taken the opportunity for you to be a leveraged person that is more valuable than just their time away as well. So I think that's one piece that drives a lot of failures, just this like, "Okay. Now, I have more problems to work on. I'm going to go deeper on it," and handing the people on your team the least interesting, least leveraged, least fun stuff to do, thinking that's how you get to like, "Oh, now, I get to work on the fun projects, and the interesting and high-leverage ones, and I'll leave all the other ones to other people."
turns.zh: 因此，从一个角度来说，是的，这可能是近期你应该关注的正确的事情，并致力于此，并真正指导要做什么，并了解每一个细节，并确保交付最好的产品。但从长远来看，你从别人那里夺走了学习的机会，并且你抓住了这个机会，让自己成为一个比他们离开的时间更有价值的人。所以我认为这是导致很多失败的一个因素，就像，“好吧。现在，我有更多的问题需要解决。我要更深入地研究它”，并把最不有趣、最没有杠杆作用、最无趣的事情交给团队中的人去做，认为这就是你喜欢的方式，“哦，现在，我开始从事有趣的项目，以及有趣和高杠杆率的项目，我会把所有其他的项目留给其他人。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you call this the manager death spiral. Is that the same?
turns.zh: 我想你称之为经理死亡螺旋。是一样的吗？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, manager death spiral.
turns.zh: 是的。是的，经理死亡螺旋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: This is not unique to product management. This happens in almost every leadership role. You're in a position. You have broader responsibility. You got there by being the best IC on the team probably, so your instincts are to, "I see a bunch of important stuff," and do management stuff too. Right?
turns.zh: 这并不是产品管理所独有的。几乎每个领导角色都会发生这种情况。你处于一个位置。你有更广泛的责任。你可能是团队中最好的 IC，所以你的直觉是，“我看到了很多重要的东西”，并且也做管理工作。正确的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People may be like, "Oh, shit. How do I avoid this death spiral?" Do you have any advice? Maybe you'll get there, but just how do you avoid this death spiral of keeping all the good stuff and just not scaling yourself?
turns.zh: 人们可能会说，“哦，糟糕。我该如何避免这种死亡螺旋呢？”你有什么建议吗？也许你会到达那里，但你如何避免这种保留所有好东西而不扩展自己的死亡螺旋呢？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: I think the first is, honestly, just you have to start trusting other people, which is not common to where you've been till today, but you have to start trusting. You have to shift from doer to editor is the way I think about it. You have to shift from, "My job is to do the work," to, "My job is to make the work better. My job is to plus the work, to review the work, to help other people solve problem." Sometimes that's by being directive. Right?
turns.zh: 老实说，我认为第一是你必须开始信任其他人，这在你今天所处的地方并不常见，但你必须开始信任。我的想法是，你必须从实干者转变为编辑者。你必须从“我的工作是做工作”转变为“我的工作是让工作变得更好。我的工作是补充工作、审查工作、帮助其他人解决问题”。有时这是通过指导。正确的？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Sometimes that's by letting them run because you're like, "Lenny, you're great. Please go solve this problem. Call me when you have a problem." If you have people that are in that upper quadrant of like they understand the problem, they have the level of experience to solve it, it's maybe not 100% important. Maybe it is. That kind of thing. Then, there's the coach in the middle, which is like, "How do I help make that work better?" They have to start figuring out like, "Where is each person on your team in their expertise, and what level of input is the highest leverage for me?"
turns.zh: 有时这是让他们运行，因为你会说，“莱尼，你很棒。请去解决这个问题。有问题时给我打电话。”如果你的人处于上象限，他们了解问题，他们有解决问题的经验，那么这可能不是 100% 重要。也许是的。那种事。然后，中间是教练，他的意思是，“我如何帮助让这项工作变得更好？”他们必须开始弄清楚，“团队中每个人的专业知识处于什么位置，什么水平的投入对我来说是最高的影响力？”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: I actually think of it as start thinking in terms of being lazy, "What's the least amount of work I could do to make this thing as good as possible?" versus, "How do I do as much work as possible to make sure it's great?" So it's like looking in terms of ROI. The other is just hiring, bringing on great people you trust, making sure you're staffed appropriately, and there's just a second bit. I think one of the bigger mistakes that new ICs make on teams, that they still treat problems the same way they did as ICs, which normally, when you run a pod, basically, your job is, "How do I deliver the most value with the resources I have?"
turns.zh: 我实际上认为这是开始从懒惰的角度思考，“我可以做的最少工作量是多少，才能让这件事尽可能好？”与“我如何做尽可能多的工作以确保它很棒？”所以这就像关注投资回报率。另一个就是招聘，引进你信任的优秀人才，确保你配备适当的人员，还有第二点。我认为新 IC 在团队中犯下的更大错误之一是，他们仍然以与 IC 相同的方式处理问题，通常，当你运行一个 Pod 时，基本上，你的工作是，“我如何利用我拥有的资源提供最大的价值？”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: When you're a leader, it's now your job to propose, "What are the resources we need to have the most impact on this problem?" I think I personally have messed this up a bunch of times where at the end of the core, I'll be like, "Yeah, but we only had four engineers, and this is what we could do." I'm like, "That wasn't what we asked you to do. We asked you to solve this problem. So adding four more people was what you needed or you needed the marketing team to do X, Y, and Z." You need to go out and do that work now. It is not just your job to get what you can get done with the resources in front of you. It's your job to marshal resources both inside your org and across your organization. I think that's another big area that's related to the trust bit because, again, it's this habit of, "Oh, I got here by doing everything myself." You have to start realizing that your job is to convince other people to do work too.
turns.zh: 当你是领导者时，你现在的工作就是提出“我们需要哪些资源才能对这个问题产生最大的影响？”我想我个人已经把这件事搞砸了很多次，在核心结束时，我会说，“是的，但我们只有四名工程师，这就是我们能做的。”我说，“这不是我们要求你做的。我们要求你解决这个问题。所以你需要再增加四个人，或者你需要营销团队来做 X、Y 和 Z。”你现在需要出去做这项工作。利用你面前的资源完成你能完成的事情不仅仅是你的工作。您的工作是整理组织内部和整个组织的资源。我认为这是与信任相关的另一个重要领域，因为这又是一种习惯，“哦，我自己做所有事情才来到这里。”你必须开始意识到你的工作就是说服其他人也去做工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So, going back to the canyon. So the first piece was essentially over-focusing on just being too good at the thing you're already doing versus going broader, is that right?
turns.zh: 惊人的。于是，又回到了峡谷。因此，第一部分本质上是过度关注于在你已经在做的事情上做得太好，而不是更广泛，对吗？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Mm-hmm. Yeah. So it's like, "Hey, how do I maximize my output? I can do this myself faster than I can explain it to someone else, so I'll just do it," and then finding that you're blocking your team because you're in the middle of every single decision, finding that you're totally overworked, and finding that people aren't learning or growing because those opportunities have been taken from them. So what do you do to break that? You have to just slowly start to give up, trust, do that. So I think that's the one bit is that death spiral of what's getting stuff done.
turns.zh: 嗯嗯。是的。所以这就像是，“嘿，我如何最大化我的产出？我自己做这件事的速度比我向别人解释它的速度要快，所以我就这样做，”然后发现你阻碍了你的团队，因为你在每一个决策中，发现你完全工作过度，发现人们没有学习或成长，因为这些机会已经被剥夺了。那么你要做什么来打破这个呢？你必须慢慢开始放弃、相信、去做。所以我认为这就是完成工作的死亡螺旋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, no. You can curse all you want. That's all good.
turns.zh: 不，不。你可以随心所欲地咒骂。这一切都很好。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Okay. Great. Oh, you've just... Well, be careful with "all you want."
turns.zh: 好的。伟大的。哦，你刚刚……好吧，小心“你想要的一切”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nobody has cursed yet on this podcast, and it's all allowed.
turns.zh: 还没有人在这个播客上咒骂过，这都是允许的。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's the internet. I don't know.
turns.zh: 这是互联网。我不知道。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: We'll solve that.
turns.zh: 我们会解决这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Don't worry. I think the other is what I call the four types of product work, and I think this is not always right at the manager stage. But for every great product leader, you go from being an expert in some type of product work, and I'll describe what those are, to now owning a portfolio of work across a bunch of different dimensions. So the way I think about product work, and Casey Winters and I worked on this framework together, a lot of it comes from him. So I don't want to oversay it, but it's all part of our product strategy program at Reforge is first, feature work, adding new features, product experiences, et cetera into a product in order to drive engagement with your existing customer base and solve a wider range of problems.
turns.zh: 不用担心。我认为另一个就是我所说的四类产品工作，我认为这在经理阶段并不总是正确的。但对于每一位伟大的产品领导者来说，你都会从某种类型的产品工作的专家（我将描述这些是什么），到现在拥有跨多个不同维度的工作组合。所以我对产品工作的思考方式，以及我和 Casey Winters 一起开发这个框架的方式，很多都来自于他。所以我不想过分强调，但这都是我们 Reforge 产品战略计划的一部分，首先是功能工作，在产品中添加新功能、产品体验等，以推动与现有客户群的互动并解决更广泛的问题。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: The second is growth work. "How do I help my customers or a broader range of customers connect with the experiences we already have, and drive acceleration and either top-line growth, or modernization, or whatever the most important metrics are. I think you've had many guests on to talk about growth type work. The third is related to growth, but I think is slightly different, which is what we call product market fit expansion. So it's not exactly feature work, which is like, "Hey, now that I use your product more, I have this thing I need in order to keep using it because I'm a power seller," those kinds of things. But instead, we want to attract a whole new sub-segments of markets to the product by adding something.
turns.zh: 二是成长工作。 “我如何帮助我的客户或更广泛的客户与我们已有的体验建立联系，并推动加速以及营收增长、现代化或任何最重要的指标。我想你们已经有很多嘉宾谈论了增长型工作。第三个与增长有关，但我认为略有不同，这就是我们所说的产品市场适应扩展。所以这不完全是功能工作，就像，“嘿，现在我更多地使用你的产品，我有这个东西我需要继续使用它，因为我是一个超级卖家，”诸如此类的事情。但相反，我们希望通过添加一些东西来为产品吸引全新的细分市场。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: There are two forms of product market fit expansion. There's either taking the same product and finding a new audience. Things like internationalization or vertical like, "I'm going to sell the same product to a different vertical because we're a verticalized product." The other is selling a different product to the same audience. This is what bundling strategies basically look like. Right? So adding new marketing tools to a marketing suite, et cetera that attract a different kind of customer and that either drive upsell or drive new audiences to come to that.
turns.zh: 产品市场契合拓展有两种形式。要么采用相同的产品并寻找新的受众。像国际化或垂直化之类的事情，“我将把相同的产品销售给不同的垂直领域，因为我们是垂直化产品。”另一种是向相同的受众销售不同的产品。这就是捆绑策略的基本样子。正确的？因此，在营销套件中添加新的营销工具等等，以吸引不同类型的客户，并推动追加销售或吸引新受众。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So that's the third kind of product work, and then there's the fourth that is always forgotten by a lot of PMs which is scaling work. So what is the stuff we're doing that is because we are growing, there's new product work we need to do? Most people think of this as technical scaling, but I actually put things like trust, and safety, and other kinds of what we call user scaling problems in this as well. There are a lot of problems that come up at Airbnb just because instead of having 10 hosts, you have 10,000 hosts. Right? There are a lot of problems at Twitter and Facebook that are well puzzle-sized that are a result of their scale, and I think that's a chunk of work that I put in the same category as technical scaling, which is like, "How do we make sure the product continues to work for the people who are using it?"
turns.zh: 这是第三种产品工作，第四种产品工作总是被很多 PM 忘记，那就是扩展工作。那么，我们正在做的事情是因为我们在成长，我们需要做新的产品工作？大多数人认为这是技术扩展，但实际上我也将信任、安全以及其他类型的用户扩展问题也纳入其中。 Airbnb 会出现很多问题，因为您的房东不再是 10 名，而是 10,000 名。正确的？ Twitter 和 Facebook 存在很多由于其规模而难以解决的问题，我认为这是我将其与技术扩展归为同一类别的大量工作，就像“我们如何确保产品继续为使用它的人服务？”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So the challenge of the four kinds of product work. "Okay. Great. We have a framework. How is that useful, Fareed?" It's not that useful. It is to know what kind you're doing, but I think as you go up the stack of product leadership, you are going from being probably an expert in one of these, so for me, growth, to needing to think about all these other ones, and you've probably never done them before. Right? Maybe you've done two, but how do you lead across a bunch of different things, and how do you make sure not to be over-focused on the one that you care the most about?
turns.zh: 那么四种产品工作的挑战。 “好吧。太好了。我们有一个框架。它有什么用，法里德？”这没那么有用。是为了知道你在做什么，但我认为当你在产品领导层中晋升时，你可能会从成为其中一个方面的专家（所以对我来说，成长），到需要考虑所有其他方面，而你以前可能从未做过这些事情。正确的？也许您已经做了两件事，但是您如何领导一堆不同的事情，以及如何确保不会过度关注您最关心的事情？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: We've all seen this. Right? It's like growth leader takes over, and everything is a growth problem. Everything is an experiment. Everything should be measured. That's not necessarily true for some of these other kinds of work, and so how do you start to lead, and grow, and build a portfolio across those? I think that's where some of the stuff we talked about before, deep curiosity, looking across, asking a lot of questions, getting to a foundational understanding of what's important there, et cetera is really important.
turns.zh: 我们都看到了这一点。正确的？这就好像增长领导者接管了一切，一切都是增长问题。一切都是一个实验。一切都应该衡量。对于其他一些类型的工作来说，情况不一定如此，那么您如何开始领导、发展并建立跨这些工作的投资组合呢？我认为这就是我们之前讨论过的一些东西，深刻的好奇心，放眼世界，提出很多问题，对重要的事情有一个基本的了解等等，这些都是非常重要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So part of this is learning new types of product work. So we're talking about trying to move from IC to manager and the things that get in the way, and so is the advice there just start to learn and understand... Maybe, say, you're doing feature work. You're just building a dashboard for your users. Is your advice there like start thinking about how growth works and understand the growth strategy of the company so that people give you this opportunity of, "Okay. Let's put Fareed on maybe a couple other things here because he already understands a little bit more about growth?"
turns.zh: 知道了。因此，其中一部分就是学习新类型的产品工作。所以我们正在谈论尝试从 IC 转向经理以及阻碍的事情，因此那里的建议只是开始学习和理解......也许，比如说，你正在做功能工作。您只是为您的用户构建一个仪表板。你的建议是开始思考增长如何运作并了解公司的增长战略，以便人们给你这个机会，“好吧。让我们让法里德在这里讲一些其他的事情，因为他已经对增长有了更多的了解？”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah. I think there's a framework thing, and then there's like, "What practical advice?" So from a framework perspective, I think it's important to ask the question, "For each of the things that I am responsible for, what category does this fall into? What's important about it? What are the right ways to think about building that, given that it is different than what I've built before?" So, some of this, you can do within an org. If you're working on core product stuff, you probably have an adoption problem on one of your products, and there's growth work associated with driving usage of that thing.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为有一个框架，然后就是“什么实用建议？”因此，从框架的角度来看，我认为提出这样一个问题很重要：“对于我负责的每件事，它属于什么类别？它的重要之处是什么？考虑到它与我之前构建的内容不同，思考构建它的正确方法是什么？”因此，其中一些工作可以在组织内完成。如果您正在开发核心产品，那么您的其中一款产品可能会遇到采用问题，并且需要进行与推动该产品的使用相关的增长工作。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So I think there's a piece at which even within a certain sub-segment that this can be valuable. You could be working on enterprise, which looks a lot like a lot of scaling work, right, and a lot of feature work, "Get me the right administrative dashboards and these kinds of things," but also, maybe you have a problem that's a growth problem. "How do I drive adoption? How do I actually drive usage? How do I make sure that our new enterprise customers are activated and retained?"
turns.zh: 所以我认为即使在某个细分市场中，这也是有价值的。您可能正在从事企业工作，这看起来很像大量的扩展工作，对吧，还有很多功能工作，“给我提供正确的管理仪表板和诸如此类的事情”，但是，也许您遇到了一个增长问题。 “如何推动采用？如何真正推动使用？如何确保激活并保留我们的新企业客户？”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So I think at scale, any product leadership work has some pieces of these different kinds, and I think building a mental model for, "What are the other things we need to do? What's the right portfolio allocation across these different types of product work, and do I have enough of a baseline understanding of the different ways to evaluate and think about those and what the goals are in order to drive leadership across work I might not be able to do myself very well?" I am not a good technical PM despite having an engineering background. It's been too long, but I hope that I can lead technical scaling, technical debt restructure on my team or at least understand whether it's important to do or not.
turns.zh: 因此，我认为，从规模上看，任何产品领导力工作都包含这些不同类型的部分，我认为建立一个心理模型，“我们还需要做哪些其他事情？在这些不同类型的产品工作中正确的投资组合分配是什么？我对评估和思考这些工作的不同方式是否有足够的基本了解，以及目标是什么，以便推动工作中的领导力，我自己可能无法做得很好？”尽管我有工程背景，但我并不是一个好的技术产品经理。时间已经太长了，但我希望我能够领导团队的技术扩展、技术债务重组，或者至少了解这样做是否重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So if you think about this concept of getting through this canyon broadly, it boils down to more scope. Maybe that's the way to think about it. It's like more scope of product work that you work on, being better at different types of work, scaling yourself so that other people can do work on your behalf or within your umbrella, and the point you made about not being satisfied with the resources you have and in helping people understand, "Here's what we could do if we had this many resources," and making the case for that feels like that's the overview. Is that how you think about it?
turns.zh: 因此，如果你从广义上考虑穿越这个峡谷的概念，它可以归结为更大的范围。也许这就是思考这个问题的方式。这就像你从事的产品工作范围更大，在不同类型的工作上做得更好，扩展自己，以便其他人可以代表你或在你的保护伞内工作，以及你提出的对你拥有的资源不满意的观点，并帮助人们理解，“如果我们有这么多资源，我们可以做这些”，并为此提供理由，感觉这就是概述。你是这么想的吗？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah. I think that's exactly right, and the last one is really important because now, you have moved to owning the impact. As a leader, you now own the business outcome, the impact, the delivery, not some sub-problem or known answer. You have to define the solutions. You have to talk about how many people you need to do them, and you need to figure out what do you need from the rest of the organization to do that. So, yeah. I think those are the three big buckets of things that I see trip people up.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为这是完全正确的，最后一个非常重要，因为现在，你已经开始拥有影响力。作为领导者，您现在负责业务成果、影响、交付，而不是某些子问题或已知答案。您必须定义解决方案。你必须谈论你需要多少人来完成这些任务，并且你需要弄清楚你需要从组织的其他成员那里得到什么来完成这些任务。所以，是的。我认为这些是我看到的让人们困惑的三大问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, and just add plus one to that last point. Just like a lot of PMs end up being victims of the resources they get and like, "Oh, how could I have possibly had this impact with the resources you gave me?" versus, "How do I avoid that and empower myself to help people understand, 'Here's what I need to do this thing that you want me to do. If you think this is important, here's what we need,' and put it on other people's plate?" It doesn't mean you'll get it, but it's important to put that up front.
turns.zh: 太棒了，只需在最后一点上加一即可。就像许多产品经理最终成为他们所获得的资源的受害者一样，“哦，我怎么可能用你给我的资源产生这种影响呢？”与“我如何避免这种情况并赋予自己力量帮助人们理解，‘这是我需要做的事情，你想让我做的事情。如果你认为这很重要，这就是我们需要的’，并将其放在其他人的盘子上？”这并不意味着您会得到它，但将其放在前面很重要。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah, and that goes from a "would be nice" and makes you a better... more junior or even senior PM makes you a more effective one. It's extra credit. At the leadership level, it's baseline. The baseline is, "Okay. I believe this is the outcome we need to get to by this time, and this is what it's going to take. Here are the trade-offs. Here's what I need. Here's what I can get you if I can't do that." The reason I drum this one home is I feel like this is the mistake I have made now multiple times in my career, and I can't... At this point, I'm embarrassed to have seen it happen over and over again because you just get caught up in like, "Okay. Here's the team I have. I've got to build a roadmap. I've got to make sure everybody's got work to do," and you say focused on feeding that beast, and you forget to ask, "Is this even the right group to solve this?" Maybe you need a smaller team even, maybe you need a bigger team, or maybe you need different people. I think often, you find yourself victim of the circumstances instead of owning the situation.
turns.zh: 是的，这源于“那就太好了”，会让你成为一个更好的……更初级甚至高级的 PM 会让你成为一个更有效率的人。这是额外的学分。在领导层，这是底线。底线是，“好吧。我相信这是我们这次需要达到的结果，这就是我们将要采取的措施。这是权衡。这是我需要的。这是如果我做不到的话我可以给你的。”我之所以把这件事打回家，是因为我觉得这是我在职业生涯中多次犯下的错误，而我不能......在这一点上，我很尴尬地看到它一遍又一遍地发生，因为你只是陷入这样的境地，“好吧。这是我拥有的团队。我必须制定路线图。我必须确保每个人都有工作要做，”你说专注于喂养那头野兽，而你忘了问，“是吗？”这甚至是解决这个问题的正确小组吗？”也许您甚至需要一个较小的团队，也许您需要一个更大的团队，或者您可能需要不同的人。我认为，你经常发现自己是环境的受害者，而不是拥有环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. When did you realize this was something you should be doing?
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个。你什么时候意识到这是你应该做的事情？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: I've learned different versions of this lesson now multiple times. I learned it at Instacart. I had a very small team, and we've got a lot done. But honestly, I think I failed to make the case that we should grow it faster and only... It was only when someone was like, "We should add more people." I was like, "Great. Yeah. Let's do that." I don't think I was hurt by that, but I think it was a, "Oh, you have permission. You should have asked," kind of thing. I think at Slack, the lesson I learned was about cross-functional. I think we did a good job of making the case for why we needed new teams or add more things to drive more impact, but I still took a very product approach to solving activation and monetization expansion type problems.
turns.zh: 我已经多次学习了本课程的不同版本。我是在 Instacart 上学到的。我的团队很小，但我们完成了很多工作。但老实说，我认为我没能证明我们应该更快地发展它，而且只是……只有当有人说“我们应该增加更多的人”时。我当时想，“太好了。是的。我们就这么做吧。”我不认为我因此受到伤害，但我认为这是一种“哦，你得到了许可。你应该问一下”之类的事情。我认为在 Slack，我学到的教训是关于跨职能的。我认为我们很好地解释了为什么我们需要新的团队或添加更多的东西来产生更大的影响，但我仍然采取了一种非常产品的方法来解决激活和货币化扩展类型的问题。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: What I think is I look at what could have moved the needle more and what it could have made me a more successful leader at that company. It would've been partnering more closely with marketing, for instance, to figure out how we could be working on things together, helping drive their roadmap, and vice versa. Same with sales. Same with the data org. Same with finance. Those kinds of things where I don't think I was driving enough of the high-level outcome I owned, which is driving growth in the self-service business across the other parts of the company that needed to do that. I was a product leader, so I did product work, and I... Lesson learned.
turns.zh: 我的想法是，我会着眼于什么可以让事情变得更有意义，以及什么可以让我成为该公司更成功的领导者。例如，它将与营销部门更紧密地合作，找出我们如何共同努力，帮助推动他们的路线图，反之亦然。与销售相同。与数据组织相同。金融也一样。在这些事情上，我认为我没有充分推动我所拥有的高水平成果，而这些成果正在推动公司其他需要这样做的部门的自助服务业务的增长。我是一名产品负责人，所以我做了产品工作，我……吸取了教训。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Thanks for sharing that. So we've been talking a lot about the regular path, and getting better and accelerating your path as a product leader, and staying on this track. There's also this alternative track that I know you're passionate about, and Reforge just become a beacon, it feels like, of folks that are moving away from working at one company to working at many companies and scaling their impact. I'm curious to hear your thoughts on what you've seen there. There's this large trend of just senior people becoming advisors, writing things, newsletters, for example. I'm curious what you think is happening there and how you think about that.
turns.zh: 是的。感谢您分享这一点。因此，我们一直在谈论常规路径，以及如何变得更好并加速您作为产品领导者的道路，并保持在这条轨道上。我知道您也热衷于这种另类轨道，对于那些从一家公司工作转向在多家公司工作并扩大其影响力的人们来说，Reforge 似乎成为了一座灯塔。我很想听听您对在那里所见所闻的看法。现在的大趋势是，只有高级人才成为顾问，撰写文章、新闻通讯等。我很好奇你认为那里正在发生什么以及你对此有何看法。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: It's interesting. The whys are hard to pin down, but it's definitely happening. I think some of it is maybe COVID-induced, some of it is remote work driving these trends, and some of it is just like there are a lot more leaders who are a lot more in demand. So, just to recap, a trend that I think we are seeing and that has been really interesting is a trend of senior leaders, people with meaningful operating experience, first, diversifying their impact maybe while they're still at a full-time role. Someone like yourself, Lenny, maybe was full-time at Airbnb or a similar company and said, "Hey, I'd like to do some advising, some angel investing, some speaking. Maybe I'll start writing a newsletter on the side," and then moving to this new category that I don't feel like really existed. Maybe it did in certain pockets of executive leadership around tech and startups, but really seeing it in product management of a shift towards, "The best use of my time and my career is to work across a portfolio of problems that a variety of different companies."
turns.zh: 这很有趣。原因很难确定，但它确实正在发生。我认为其中一些可能是由新冠病毒引起的，一些是远程工作推动了这些趋势，还有一些就像有更多的领导者需要更多的东西一样。因此，回顾一下，我认为我们正在看到并且非常有趣的趋势是高级领导者的趋势，即具有有意义的运营经验的人，首先，也许在他们仍担任全职职位时就使他们的影响力多样化。像你这样的人，莱尼，可能是 Airbnb 或类似公司的全职员工，他说：“嘿，我想做一些建议，一些天使投资，一些演讲。也许我会开始写一份时事通讯，”然后转向这个我觉得并不真正存在的新类别。也许在科技和初创公司的某些高管领导层中确实如此，但在产品管理中确实看到了这一转变，“我的时间和职业生涯的最佳利用方式是解决各种不同公司面临的一系列问题。”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So we are seeing a larger percentage of our executive network. It's still small, but working on things like newsletters, podcasts, those and the like at the edge of the content creator side, but also, full-time advisors, fractional heads of growth, fractional heads of product one day a week, et cetera. Long-term advisory relationships, running workshops. These kinds of things that are more like a la carte. I think they love it because of the flexibility that it creates for them. They love it because of the high upside and non-linearity of possibility of results now instead of having equity in one company for four years of 100% of my time. It's a portfolio approach to not just the time and energy, but also the upside and opportunities that are there as well as the fact that they're just so in demand.
turns.zh: 因此，我们看到我们的高管网络中所占的比例更大。它仍然很小，但致力于新闻通讯、播客等内容创作者边缘的事情，而且还有全职顾问、增长部分负责人、每周一天的产品部分负责人等等。长期咨询关系，举办研讨会。这些东西更像是点菜。我认为他们喜欢它是因为它为他们创造了灵活性。他们喜欢它，因为现在结果的可能性具有很高的上升空间和非线性，而不是我在四年内 100% 的时间都持有一家公司的股权。这是一种投资组合方法，不仅要投入时间和精力，还要考虑其中的优势和机会，以及它们的需求如此之大的事实。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: For senior leaders who have been in meaningful seats at well-known companies, you're getting hit up by recruiters all day long, and the decision, "What do I want to spend the next four or five, six years of my life on if it's just one thing?" is a very difficult one. So what we're finding is people seeing, "Hey, you don't need me full-time. What you need is me here a day a week to help your up and coming leaders be awesome." We're just seeing more and more of that in the industry, and it's been a really interesting trend to observe. Of our executives and residents, I would say most now are exploring this kind of advisory, fractional, or otherwise portfolio-based approach to their futures. Whereas most of them came from full-time roles beforehand.
turns.zh: 对于在知名公司担任过重要职位的高级领导者来说，你整天都会受到招聘人员的骚扰，并做出这样的决定：“如果我只做一件事，我想在生命中接下来的四、五年、六年里度过什么？”是一件非常困难的事。所以我们发现人们会看到，“嘿，你不需要我全职工作。你需要的是我每周在这里帮助你的后起之秀领导者变得出色。”我们在行业中看到越来越多的这种情况，这是一个非常值得观察的有趣趋势。我想说，在我们的高管和居民中，大多数人现在正在探索这种咨询、部分或其他基于投资组合的方法来实现他们的未来。而他们中的大多数人之前都是全职工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. A program at Reforge is designed for that. The idea there is, "You don't know what you're going to do next? Come teach a class at Reforge to help some folks out, and then use that as the time to explore what you're going to do next." Right?
turns.zh: 是的。 Reforge 的一个项目就是为此而设计的。这个想法是，“你不知道下一步要做什么？来 Reforge 教一堂课来帮助一些人，然后利用这个时间来探索你下一步要做什么。”正确的？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, it is, and the hypothesis... I was one of the first EIR, so I started as an EIR at the company, and then ended up joining full-time as an executive. The hypothesis was, "Hey, let's give people six months to a year so that they don't just hop from one really high-stress, really difficult job into the next one. We also want great operators teaching and meeting our programs. How do we build a win-win situation?" So what we did was we created the Executive in Residence program as a way to help top operators have a transition point, but I think the hypothesis was that most of them would take on the next VP product role, or CPO role, or CMO type role, and what we're finding is that more and more of them are using that space and time.
turns.zh: 是的。是的，是的，假设...我是第一批 EIR 之一，所以我一开始是公司的 EIR，然后最终成为全职高管。假设是，“嘿，让我们给人们六个月到一年的时间，这样他们就不会从一个压力很大、非常困难的工作跳到下一个工作。我们还希望优秀的操作员教授和满足我们的计划。我们如何建立双赢的局面？”因此，我们所做的是创建常驻高管计划，作为帮助顶级运营商实现过渡点的一种方式，但我认为假设是他们中的大多数人将担任下一个 VP 产品角色、CPO 角色或 CMO 类型的角色，我们发现越来越多的人正在利用这些空间和时间。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: They are building up their understanding of where they're experts and what their real TEDx value is, and then finding ways to do that across a variety of different companies and organizations versus just the single one, one, because they want to try before they buy, so to speak, in terms of of like even if you do end up somewhere full-time, it's nice to be able to really work with them and get to know them because at the executive level in particular, it's a really high level of commitment, and you have a lot of opportunities, so you want to be really careful about it. But also, two, because it may not be the best use of your energy. When you have a lot of frameworks and you have a lot of broad understanding, you have a lot of examples, your value to the ecosystem is often by helping lots of companies be successful, not just one. I suspect that's how you feel about what you're doing as well.
turns.zh: 他们正在逐渐了解自己的专家身份以及他们真正的 TEDx 价值是什么，然后寻找方法在各种不同的公司和组织中做到这一点，而不是单一的公司和组织，因为他们想在购买之前尝试一下，可以这么说，即使你最终在某个地方全职工作，能够真正与他们合作并了解他们也是很好的，因为特别是在高管层面，这是一种非常高水平的承诺，而且你有很多机会， so you want to be really careful about it. But also, two, because it may not be the best use of your energy.当你有很多框架并且有很多广泛的理解时，你有很多例子，你对生态系统的价值通常是帮助很多公司取得成功，而不仅仅是一家公司。 I suspect that's how you feel about what you're doing as well.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. When I started down this path of experimenting with a newsletter back in the day, I called it Project Avoid Getting a Real Job, and what I was trying to do is figure out, "Can I make a living doing this thing even though I don't know if there's any way to make money writing a thing?" My wife is always like, "There's no money in writing. What are you doing? I thought you wanted to start a company, that you wanted to do some advising."
turns.zh: 是的。当我开始尝试时事通讯时，我把它称为“避免找到真正的工作项目”，而我想做的是弄清楚，“即使我不知道写东西是否有办法赚钱，我可以靠做这件事谋生吗？”我妻子总是说，“写作没钱。你在做什么？我以为你想开一家公司，你想做一些建议。”

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah. Well, let me talk about why I think the generalization there's no money in writing is true, but I think it's true because it's... In general, maybe not, but what's happening, I think, is people are figuring out, "What is my specific knowledge," just to tie the knots back to the thing we started at the beginning, "that because I've taken so many reps at this is actually not easily replaceable in a focused area?" So modernization or building zero-to-one paid channels as a marketer, or whatever it is. Just narrow enough that I know I'm one of the five best in the world at or I can make the case that I'm one of the five best in the world at it. You as a company probably can't hire that person because you're too early, don't have enough money, don't have enough clout, et cetera, and that I have generalized enough in my mind that I can actually be really effective in a small amount of time.
turns.zh: 是的。好吧，让我谈谈为什么我认为没有钱写的概括是正确的，但我认为这是正确的，因为……总的来说，也许不是，但我认为正在发生的事情是人们正在弄清楚，“我的具体知识是什么”，只是为了将结带回到我们一开始就开始的事情，“因为我在这方面做了这么多次代表，所以在一个重点领域实际上不容易被替换？”因此，作为营销人员进行现代化或建立零到一的付费渠道，或者其他什么。只要范围足够小，我就知道我是世界上最好的五个人之一，或者我可以证明我是世界上最好的五个人之一。作为一家公司，你可能无法雇用那个人，因为你太早了，没有足够的钱，没有足够的影响力，等等，而且我已经在头脑中进行了足够的概括，我实际上可以在很短的时间内真正有效。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So what works for you, I don't know a lot about the mechanics of your newsletter, but it's not just writing. You're writing about a very specific set of topics that you have unique experience in that has harnessed a very focused community, and I think we're seeing this across a bunch of different things that there's a lot of sub-expertise. No one can be an expert at company. Some people claim to be, but when you get down to it, I feel like an expert on bottoms-up SaaS activation strategy is like, "I can speak pretty confidently about that. Somebody has a problem in that space, I can usually at an hour accelerate their learning pretty dramatically." I think as we're finding what these things are and people are getting smarter about what they're looking for, I think it opened up this space where you can be the best in the world at a relatively narrow topic and make a real meaningful living out of it.
turns.zh: So what works for you, I don't know a lot about the mechanics of your newsletter, but it's not just writing.你正在写一组非常具体的主题，你在这些主题上拥有独特的经验，并且利用了一个非常专注的社区，我认为我们在许多不同的事情上看到了这一点，其中有很多子专业知识。 No one can be an expert at company.有些人声称是，但当你认真对待它时，我觉得自下而上的 SaaS 激活策略专家会说，“我可以非常自信地谈论这一点。有人在这个领域遇到问题，我通常可以在一个小时内极大地加快他们的学习速度。”我认为，随着我们正在发现这些东西是什么，人们对他们正在寻找的东西变得越来越聪明，我认为它打开了这个空间，在这里你可以在一个相对狭窄的主题上成为世界上最好的，并从中过上真正有意义的生活。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's two thoughts I want to go into here, and then I think we should probably wrap up, but one is I do worry there's like... everyone that gets to a certain point, it just exits the career track, and who's left to build things? I worry that just everyone is trying to become an influencer/creator person. So what I wanted to chat about briefly is just downsides of this path in life.
turns.zh: 我想在这里谈两个想法，然后我想我们应该结束了，但一个是我确实担心……每个人到达某一点后，就会退出职业轨道，剩下谁来构建东西？我担心每个人都想成为有影响力的人/创造者。所以我想简单谈谈这条人生道路的缺点。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other pieces is for folks listening that want to pursue this direction, what could they do to set themselves up? So the first piece is just like, what are the downsides? I'll share a few already. So in this life that I lead now, I get no health insurance benefits. I get no time off. I get no 401(k) matching. None of that. I have to basically pay an absurd amount of money for health insurance and find ways to take time off, invent PTO policies for myself, and all these sorts of things. I've gotten used to it, but it is weird. My wife is also an independent self-employed person, so we both don't have... If we have a child, we have no mat leave, pat leave. We just have to figure that out. I don't know how I would do that. So that comes to mind for me. What else have you seen as the downside of this path?
turns.zh: 其他的作品是为那些想要追求这个方向的人准备的，他们可以做些什么来让自己做好准备？所以第一部分就像，有什么缺点？ I'll share a few already.所以在我现在的生活中，我没有得到任何健康保险福利。我没有时间休息。 I get no 401(k) matching.都不是。我基本上必须为健康保险支付一大笔荒唐的钱，并找到休假的方法，为自己制定 PTO 政策，以及所有这些事情。我已经习惯了，但还是很奇怪。我老婆也是独立个体户，所以我们俩都没有……如果有了孩子，我们就没有席假、拍假。 We just have to figure that out. I don't know how I would do that. So that comes to mind for me.您认为这条道路还有哪些缺点？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Yeah, the second is it's unclear what the longevity is. How far can you be removed from your full-time experience and still be valuable? This is why I actually think this is a better path than what used to happen, which is all the great operators turned into VCs, venture capitalists. Right? In there, you're pretty disconnected from the ops. I think this advisory type path, I'll leave the creator piece alone because I'm not as familiar with it. But in the advisor path, you are still maybe spending a day a week with these companies. You are still doing. You are helping grow the next generation. I don't like to say generation, but next crop of up and coming leaders. So the question mark for me is longevity. Is it possible to build more and more amazing companies if more and more amazing operators are leaving the full-time workforce?
turns.zh: 是的，第二个是不清楚寿命是什么。你的全职工作经历能离开多远，但仍然有价值？这就是为什么我实际上认为这是一条比过去更好的道路，过去所有伟大的运营商都变成了风险投资家、风险投资家。正确的？在那里，你与操作人员完全脱节。我认为这种咨询类型的路径，我将保留创作者的作品，因为我对它不太熟悉。但在顾问之路上，你可能仍然每周花一天时间与这些公司打交道。你还在做。 You are helping grow the next generation.我不想说一代人，而是下一代的新领导人。 So the question mark for me is longevity.如果越来越多出色的经营者离开全职员工队伍，是否有可能建立越来越出色的公司？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: I don't know, but I hope that it's better than what it's been because actually, they're building and doing, et cetera. So I think that's the other question mark and downside, and I think we think about this as part of our ecosystem. I think as long as people are doing, and generalizing, and executing, as I talked about it at the beginning, I think they can still be valuable in a meaningful way and maybe provide access to that kind of knowledge for a broader range of companies. The other is just like if everybody does it, then maybe it's not so unique anymore. So I think there's a question there as well.
turns.zh: 我不知道，但我希望它比以前更好，因为实际上，他们正在建造和做，等等。所以我认为这是另一个问号和缺点，我认为我们将其视为我们生态系统的一部分。我认为只要人们在做、概括和执行，正如我在一开始谈到的那样，我认为他们仍然可以以有意义的方式有价值，并且可能为更广泛的公司提供获取此类知识的机会。另一种情况是，如果每个人都这样做，那么也许它就不再那么独特了。所以我认为那里也存在一个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other piece is like you're constantly having to do sales and BD as an advisor like, "Who's the next company?" You're always wondering if there will be more, if they stopped. It's a real part of it.
turns.zh: 另一件事情就像你作为顾问经常需要做销售和业务拓展，比如“下一家公司是谁？”你总是想知道如果他们停止的话是否还会有更多。这是它真实的一部分。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: That's why it has not been attractive to me personally, I will say. I like being focused on a singular problem for some amount of time. I do a lot of portfolio-type stuff outside. I advise casually. I do some coaching. Not coaching exactly, but mentorship for a couple of different up and coming product leaders. I do some angel investing, those kinds of things. I like to see what's happening around me, but I do like having an anchor. That's like my main thing, and I don't like selling. It turns out I don't, and so you have to like that, I think, to do some of this stuff. But I think there are things our platform at Reforge will be able to do for these kinds of offers. There's a long period of time to make that easier and easier. No promises, but stay tuned.
turns.zh: 我会说，这就是为什么它对我个人没有吸引力。我喜欢在一段时间内专注于一个单一的问题。我在外面做了很多投资组合类型的事情。我随意建议。我做一些辅导。确切地说，不是辅导，而是对几个不同的后起之秀的产品领导者的指导。我做一些天使投资之类的事情。我喜欢看看周围发生的事情，但我确实喜欢有一个锚。这就是我的主要工作，我不喜欢销售。事实证明我不喜欢，所以我想你必须喜欢这样才能做一些这样的事情。但我认为我们的 Reforge 平台能够为此类优惠做一些事情。需要很长一段时间才能让这一切变得越来越容易。没有承诺，但请继续关注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, okay. So then, going back maybe as a final question. For folks that are just like, "That sounds great. Maybe in the future, I want to become a full-time advisor, EIR person, writer person," what advice do you have for folks to set their career up for a place where they can get to a place where they can become full-time advisors, let's say?
turns.zh: 好吧，好吧。那么，也许可以作为最后一个问题来回顾一下。对于那些“听起来不错。也许将来，我想成为一名全职顾问、EIR 人员、作家”的人来说，您对他们有什么建议，可以帮助他们建立自己的职业生涯，让他们能够成为全职顾问？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: This is this generalized step I talked about in the learn loop. It becomes even more important if what you want to do is not just do your current job well, but be able to communicate why that expertise is valuable to other people, other companies across a wide range of things. So I would say choose your opportunities carefully to be building the right balance of depth and breadth across different things. You need to connect dots, so you do need different data points from different types of product work and different types of organizations because you don't want to be so narrow that only DDC eCommerce company that sell once-a-year purchases or whatever is the only thing you can work on. That's just an example. I could have come up with a bunch of others.
turns.zh: 这是我在学习循环中谈到的通用步骤。如果你想做的不仅仅是做好当前的工作，而且能够向其他人、其他公司传达为什么这种专业知识对其他人、其他公司很有价值，那么这一点就变得更加重要。所以我想说，仔细选择机会，在不同事物之间建立深度和广度的适当平衡。您需要将点连接起来，因此您确实需要来自不同类型的产品工作和不同类型的组织的不同数据点，因为您不希望范围如此狭窄，以至于只有销售一年一次的采购或其他任何东西的 DDC 电子商务公司是您唯一可以做的事情。这只是一个例子。我本可以想出很多其他的。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: You need to have some breadth, right, but it's like same problem, different industry. It's one way to think about depth that's focused. Different problem, same industry is another way to think about it, but you have to come up with a unique intersection that is clearly you are in the top tier of the people who know how to do that. That's a little bit nuanced. There's an art to it I think in some respects, but I think that's an important piece of the puzzle.
turns.zh: 你需要有一定的广度，对吧，但这就像同一个问题，不同的行业。这是思考聚焦深度的一种方式。不同的问题，同一行业是另一种思考方式，但你必须想出一个独特的交集，清楚地表明你是知道如何做到这一点的人中的佼佼者。这有点微妙。我认为在某些方面这是一门艺术，但我认为这是这个难题的重要组成部分。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: Second, work at great places. I think this is good advice for almost all product managers in particular, but really, anybody working in tech, for better or for worse, where you worked matters to people for two reasons. One, it's easier to do great work at a place that is fundamentally working. When the tide is rising, there are tons of opportunities to make meaningful, deep, awesome impact. The second is what you talked about. You're going to be in the sales business eventually, and it's a lot easier to sell experience at places people have heard of than places nobody has heard of. Unfortunately, that's I think a big piece of this puzzle as well. I don't have to spend a lot of time talking about what Slack is. You probably don't have to spend a lot of time talking about what Airbnb is. I think that helps, and it is a meaningful piece of the puzzle.
turns.zh: 其次，在好地方工作。我认为这对几乎所有产品经理来说都是一个很好的建议，但实际上，任何从事科技工作的人，无论好坏，你工作的地方对人们都很重要，原因有两个。第一，在一个基本运转良好的地方更容易做出出色的工作。当潮水上涨时，就有大量机会产生有意义、深刻、令人敬畏的影响。第二个就是你说的情况。你最终将从事销售业务，在人们听说过的地方销售经验比在没人听说过的地方销售经验要容易得多。不幸的是，我认为这也是这个难题的重要组成部分。我不必花很多时间谈论 Slack 是什么。您可能不需要花很多时间谈论 Airbnb 是什么。我认为这很有帮助，而且是拼图中有意义的一块。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. Fareed, I feel like anybody that listen to this episode is going to be a better product manager. I'm very confident of that, and I'm really appreciative.
turns.zh: 绝对地。 Fareed，我觉得任何听过这集的人都会成为更好的产品经理。我对此非常有信心，也非常感激。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: I hope so.
turns.zh: 我希望如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm sure of it. So, just to close, where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, learn more, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 我确信这一点。那么，最后，如果人们想联系、了解更多信息，可以在哪里找到您，以及听众如何对您有用？

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: You can find me on Twitter almost most days, F-A-R-3-3-D. That's been my handle since I was a young man.
turns.zh: 几乎大多数时候你都可以在 Twitter 上找到我，F-A-R-3-3-D。从我年轻的时候起，这就是我的把柄。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So complicated.
turns.zh: 太复杂了。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: So check me out there. It's just threes instead at Es, right? That's probably my social network of choice and best place to communicate or hear what I'm thinking about or what I'm doing. Obviously, I do a ton of work at Reforge. On our events, I toast a bunch of different things, do a lot of stuff. If you're interested in these kinds of topics, please, I don't want to make this a sales pitch, but we have a lot of programs that are dedicated to deep dives into the problems that we've talked about here. I'm dedicating this next chapter of my career to helping a wider range of product leaders be great at their jobs, and that's what we do for a living. I hope that we can help folks there.
turns.zh: 所以检查我那里。在 Es 就只有三分，对吧？这可能是我选择的社交网络，也是交流或听到我在想什么或在做什么的最佳场所。显然，我在 Reforge 做了很多工作。在我们的活动中，我干了很多不同的事情，做了很多事情。如果您对此类主题感兴趣，请，我不想将其作为推销，但我们有很多项目致力于深入探讨我们在这里讨论的问题。我将在职业生涯的下一个篇章中致力于帮助更广泛的产品领导者出色地完成工作，而这正是我们的谋生之道。我希望我们可以帮助那里的人们。

turns.speaker: Fareed Mosavat
turns.en: As to what people can help me with, I don't know. I'm always looking for people working on interesting stuff or with interesting, unique problems.
